links.comparator_used: General-purpose GPT-4 given the same simple and optimised prompts on the same CT reports
links.outcome: Accuracy of lesion classification against radiologist-assigned LI-RADS scores, and malignant vs benign classification
links.effect: LI-RADS accuracy ranged from 40.8% (Med-LMsp) to 61.3% (Med-LMop) at lesion level and from 27.7% (Med-LMsp) to 52.4% (Med-LMop) at patient level. Malignant vs benign accuracy ranged from 56.1% (GPT-4sp) to 82.3% (Med-LMop) at lesion level and from 71.3% (Med-LMsp) to 86.5% (Med-LMop) at patient level. Med-LMop was statistically superior to the other models (all p < 0.001). Non-classification rates ranged from 12.7% (Med-LMop) to 40.5% (GPT-4sp).
links.tradeoff: Both models had high misclassification rates and inconsistent repeatability (12.7% to 39.0%), which the authors say hinder clinical use. Both models were better at detecting malignancy than at full LI-RADS classification.
links.quote: Med-LM outperforms GPT-4 in classifying liver lesions from unstructured CT reports with both models better at detecting malignancy than full LI-RADS classification.
